title: Lamport Logical Clocks: Local Increments and Message Updates
purpose: Teach how a unit-increment logical clock assigns integer timestamps to local events and message receives, and why a smaller timestamp alone does not prove that one event causally preceded another.
scope: A bounded two-process send/receive trace with integer logical clocks. We compute the receiver's updated clock as max(local, message timestamp) + 1 and compare timestamps. We do not model physical time, clock drift, or full distributed-system synchronization.
intuition: Each process keeps a counter. A local event bumps it by one. When a message arrives, the receiver's counter jumps to one more than the larger of its own counter and the message's timestamp, so the receive is stamped after both the send and any earlier local events.
learning_objectives: Compute a receiver's updated logical clock from its local clock and an incoming message timestamp using max(local, message) + 1.
Explain why observing timestamp(a) < timestamp(b) does not by itself establish that a happened before b.
prerequisites: Basic integer arithmetic and the max function
Familiarity with the idea of processes exchanging messages
assumptions: Each process increments its clock by exactly one per local event (unit increment).
Messages carry the sender's current logical timestamp and are delivered without loss.
limitations: Logical clocks give a partial order; they do not measure real elapsed time or synchronize physical clocks.
The lesson shows one bounded send/receive step, not a full distributed execution or total-order tie-breaking.
misconception: A smaller logical timestamp does not prove that the earlier-stamped event caused or happened before the later-stamped event; independent processes can produce timestamps in any relative order.
edge_cases: If the message timestamp is smaller than the receiver's local clock, the receiver still advances to local + 1.
If the message timestamp is larger, the receiver jumps to message + 1, skipping intermediate values.

inputs.name: local_clock
inputs.label: Receiver local clock L
inputs.meaning: The receiver's logical clock value just before the message is received.

inputs.name: message_timestamp
inputs.label: Message timestamp M
inputs.meaning: The sender's logical clock value carried by the arriving message.

inputs.name: send_timestamp
inputs.label: Send event timestamp S
inputs.meaning: The logical timestamp assigned to the send event at the sender.

steps.name: receiver_max
steps.label: max(L, M)
steps.expression: local_clock if local_clock > message_timestamp else message_timestamp
steps.meaning: Take the larger of the receiver's local clock and the incoming message timestamp, so the receive is not stamped before either.

steps.name: receive_clock
steps.label: Updated receiver clock
steps.meaning: Add one unit for the receive event, giving the receiver's new logical clock value.

steps.name: send_before_receive
steps.label: Send timestamp < receive timestamp
steps.meaning: Check the clock condition for this message: the send event's timestamp must be strictly less than the receive event's timestamp.

steps.name: timestamp_gap
steps.label: Receive minus send
steps.meaning: The numeric difference between the receive and send timestamps, showing how far the receiver advanced past the send.

visuals.question: How do the receiver's local clock, the message timestamp, and the updated receive clock compare?
Does the send timestamp remain strictly less than the receive timestamp after the update?

explorations.title: Message timestamp dominates
explorations.why: When the message timestamp exceeds the local clock, the receiver jumps to message + 1, so the receive is stamped after the send and the gap is one unit.

explorations.title: Local clock dominates
explorations.why: When the local clock exceeds the message timestamp, the receiver still advances to local + 1, so the receive is stamped after the send even though the message timestamp is smaller.
